6.0.s.en: (1) The trespass offering for an error toward others

6.0.1.en: That which was delivered him to keep (a found thing): belongings that fell from one person and another person found, picked up and took.

6.0.2.en: The trespass here is directed against a person, but it also contains a breaking of God's commandments, so because of the gravity of this sin the Law counts it a trespass and not an ordinary sin, and it is such as:

6.0.3.en: 1- Theft of a deposit: if a person places money or belongings with another, and the other afterward denies that they are with him and takes them for himself.

6.0.4.en: 2- Theft of a trust: such as robbing minors of their rights by their guardians, and dishonesty in buying and selling, or the dishonesty of the worker in the perfection of his work or exaggeration in demanding his wage, and likewise the reverse: the employer's reducing the worker's wage and delaying giving him his wage.

6.0.5.en: 3- Robbery: what is meant is stealing from others in secret and then denying what was stolen.

6.0.6.en: 4- Seizure: what is meant is theft by compulsion and refusal to return what was stolen.

6.0.7.en: 5- Taking a found thing: a person takes what he finds on the road or in any place, though it is not his own but belongs to others, and then denies that he took anything, and even swears to it.

6.0.8.en: The word "unwittingly" is not mentioned, because the rights of people are clear.

6.0.9.en: Here we notice that a person's spirit and body and all his abilities are a trust from God, and we are stewards over them to use them for His glory, so it is not right for us to seize them for ourselves and use them for our own passions and base desires.

6.0.10.en: Likewise the faith delivered to us and all the teachings of the Church are a trust from God, and we are bound to teach them accurately to others and not to add to them or change them according to our own ideas.

6.0.11.en: The trespass offering signifies Christ's taking away our trespasses on the Cross, even in the hardest sins, for He bore all our sins directed toward Him or toward our brothers, mankind, and He gives us this justification in the sacraments of the Church.

6.1.0.en: In the principal: at its original value.

6.1.1.en: Here it mentions compensation by returning in full what was taken, at its value, before offering the sacrifice, because repentance is not accepted before the wrong is put right. And the addition of a fifth is compensation for the one who suffered the harm, since he suffered distress that was not only material but psychological; it is compensation for the psychological pain, and so that the wrongdoer may feel his wrong, in addition to offering the sacrifice while asking God's forgiveness.

6.2.0.en: The priest determines the value of the ram that is offered according to the measure of the sin that he committed against God, and he makes sure that this trespass occurred in its five cases mentioned before, lest it be a false accusation, and the ram is offered as a trespass offering so that God may forgive him.

6.2.1.en: Be faithful with the rights of others, so give them to them before you take your own rights, and if you borrow something from a person, return it. And be careful of the feelings of others, so do not wound anyone with condemnation or mockery, but honor all, and God will bless you and honor you.

6.3.s.en: (2) The law of the burnt offering

6.3.0.en: Hearth: the top of the bronze altar.

6.3.1.en: Here it speaks of some of the laws concerning the burnt offering mentioned in (ch. 1), and it begins by speaking of the daily burnt offering that is offered in the evening, so that the priests may learn the order of offering every sacrifice. The burnt offering remains burning on the altar from six in the evening, the time of offering the evening burnt offering, until the morning. It signifies the Christian who remains aflame with the love of God throughout the darkness of this age until the dawn of eternity.

6.4.0.en: Breeches: part of the priestly garments; they are short trousers worn under the clothes.

6.4.1.en: The priest puts on his priestly garments, which are of white linen, in order to take up the ashes of the burnt offering (Ex 28:

6.4.2.en: 40-43), and this shows the value of these ashes, which point to the body of Christ after His death on the Cross, for it is a place of the delight of the Father's heart because He endured pain to the end. Then the priest takes off his priestly garments, in which he may not go outside the tabernacle of the congregation, and puts on his ordinary clothes and carries the ashes of the burnt offering to a holy place surrounded by a wall outside the camp called the place where the ashes are poured out, that is, the place where the ashes are thrown (ch. 4:12). This is so that no one may tread on them or they be scattered in the air, since they are the remains of a holy sacrifice, just as we now honor the tomb of Christ.

6.5.0.en: The holy fire is not put out on the altar by night or by day, for the priests arrange the wood in the morning and lay the morning burnt offering on it at a time when the remains of the evening burnt offering are still burning with fire, in addition to the fire's burning with the various sacrifices.

6.5.1.en: The fire had come down from heaven at the anointing of Aaron and his sons as priests and kindled the burnt offering laid on the altar (Lev 9:24), and this fire continued until the Babylonian captivity, and then it returned in the days of Nehemiah from the well in which it had been hidden (2 Macc 1:19-36).

6.5.2.en: The fire on the altar points to the fire of the Holy Spirit, which is never extinguished in the Church forever and works in it and in its sacraments.

6.5.3.en: Often our love for God grows cold in periods of lukewarmness, but prayer makes the Holy Spirit return and always kindle in us this fire. So take care of your prayers and your reading in the Holy Bible every day, that the Holy Spirit may work in you and you may be comforted and reassured.

6.6.s.en: (3) The law of the grain offering

6.6.0.en: The priest offers the grain offering before the altar and takes a handful of its flour and its oil for God, while the frankincense, which represents prayer and worship, is taken entirely for God and burned on the altar. The handful of flour that the priest took signifies the Incarnation of Christ, who took hold of us and brought us near to the Father.

6.7.1.en: Most holy: set apart for the priests only.

6.7.2.en: The remainder of the grain offering is set apart as food for the male priests, for the male signifies spiritual manhood and striving, and this points to Communion, which only the strong strivers enjoy. They eat it in the house of the Lord because of its holiness, just as the Body and Blood of Christ are now eaten in the Church. The grain offering is to be unleavened, that is, without leaven in it, because leaven signifies evil. It is noted that the Body of Christ in the Church is leavened, since Christ bore our sins on the Cross and died for us and removed from us the punishment of sin, which leaven signifies. The rest of the grain offering is eaten by the priests, as they eat the remainder of the sin offering and the trespass offering after the fat is offered on the bronze altar.

6.8.0.en: The grain offering is holy food, so it sanctifies and blesses the one who eats it, and it signifies the grace of God given in the Sacrament of the Priesthood. And everything that touches this food is sanctified, such as the vessels in which the food is put, which are set apart for this and nothing else is eaten in them.

6.8.1.en: As for the portion of the priests from the peace offerings and the crops and the fruits offered as firstfruits, it is of a lower degree of holiness, so the whole family of the priest is permitted to eat of it, males and females, and this is in a holy place and not in the house of the Lord as with the preceding foods.

6.9.0.en: The priest would offer daily, with the morning burnt offering and the evening burnt offering, an offering as mentioned in (Ex 29:40), which is:

6.9.1.en: 1- A tenth of an ephah of fine flour mingled with oil.

6.9.2.en: 2- A fourth of a hin of wine (see the explanation in the commentary on Ex 29:38-42). For the priest too, as a man, needs to offer an offering, that is, he needs the grace of Christ. The priests would offer this offering at their consecration only, but the high priest offered it daily to show his great need of divine help. The offering of half of it in the morning and half in the evening shows the priest's constant need of God, so he offers with the morning burnt offering a tenth of an ephah of fine flour and with the evening burnt offering a tenth of an ephah of fine flour also, as the Book of Exodus shows, and the priests would offer this offering on the day of their anointing, that is, after the completion of their anointing as priests.

6.10.1.en: Baken pieces: small pieces of bread.

6.10.2.en: The grain offering of the priest is offered like the ordinary grain offering, on a metal baking pan and mixed with oil, which signifies the Holy Spirit. The grain offering is a symbol of the life of Christ on earth, who was anointed with the Holy Spirit at His baptism. The grain offering is broken into pieces to declare that Christ was pure on the outside and on the inside also, for the breaking into pieces signifies the showing of the inside.

6.11.0.en: The anointed high priest offers the grain offering in place of Aaron after his death, for it is the ordinance of the high priest, whether Aaron or the one who succeeds him.

6.12.0.en: Every offering of the priest is burned and none of it is eaten, as an indication of the priest's being wholly consecrated to the service of God, whereas of the grain offering for the people a part is offered on the altar and the rest is eaten by the priest.

6.12.1.en: Ask God's help, if you are a father or a mother or a servant, that He may give you grace in caring for those around you, so that God is the One working in you and through you and influencing the souls of those whom you shepherd.

6.13.s.en: (4) The law of the sin offering

6.13.0.en: The sin offering is slaughtered in a holy place on the north side of the bronze altar, where the burnt offering is slaughtered (ch. 1:11), because by the redemption of Christ our sins were taken away and He gave us holiness. The fat of it is offered on the altar and burned, and the rest is eaten by the priest in the house of the Lord, so that the one who offers the sacrifice is assured of the removal of his sin by the burning of part of his sacrifice on the altar and the eating of the rest of it by God's priest.

6.14.0.en: The sin offering signifies Christ, so the priest receives blessing and holiness when he eats of it, and its blood that is sprinkled on his garment is washed in a holy place to confirm its holiness.

6.15.0.en: When one of the people offers a sin offering, its fat is burned and the flesh is eaten by the priest.

6.15.1.en: If he cooks these parts in an earthen vessel, it must be broken, because it has absorbed some of its holy blood and has become holy, so it is broken and not used again for ordinary foods because it is holy and it is thrown in a clean place. But if the vessel is of bronze, it is enough to scour it and rub it and wash it to remove the traces of the sacrifice that clung to the sides of the vessel and to cast them in a clean place.

6.16.0.en: The ritual here is as explained before in (ch. 4), with the emphasis on not eating the sin offering if it is of the kind mentioned in (ch. 4:1-21), that is, offered for the sin of the priest or the congregation of the people, and likewise the two sin offerings that are offered for the high priest and then for the people on the Day of Atonement (ch. 16:11-15). That is, the sin offering whose blood is brought into the sanctuary is not eaten of at all but is burned entirely, whereas the one whose blood is not brought into the sanctuary is eaten by the priests and their male sons, and they eat it in the house of the Lord.

6.16.1.en: Reflect on the pains that our sins and uncleannesses cause our Lord Jesus Christ, the Holy One, so that you hate sin and no longer welcome it or seek to practice it.

6.16.2.en: Continuation of the laws of the sacrifices

7.0.s.en: (1) The law of the trespass offering

7.0.0.en: The trespass offering is treated like the sin offering as most holy, because it shows that Christ is holy although He bore the sins of the whole world.

7.1.0.en: All the sacrifices are slaughtered in one place on the north side of the bronze altar to declare that they are all aspects of one sacrifice, the sacrifice of Christ on the Cross, and to show its effect and its results in our lives, as mentioned in (ch. 5:14-19; ch. 6:1-7, 17). The two sacrifices are slaughtered in the same place before the Lord, that is, they bring the sinner back inside the house of God so that He is pleased with him. The blood is sprinkled round about on the bronze altar like the burnt offering, so its blood, which signifies the blood of Christ, bears the sins of the sinner for him, and the fat is burned in the same way explained before.

7.2.0.en: The priests and their male sons eat of the trespass offering as happens in the sin offering, so that the one who offers it may be assured that God has accepted it and removed His wrath from him.

7.3.0.en: The one who offers the sacrifice takes nothing of it, because it has taken away his sins, but the priest takes the skin as a second declaration to the one who offers it that God has accepted his sacrifice, and this reminds us of Adam, to whom God gave the skin to cover his nakedness and Eve's, and Adam was considered the priest of the family at that time.

7.4.0.en: After the priest offers a part of the grain offering on the altar, the priest who offered it eats the remainder of it, which is what is baked in the oven or the frying pan or on the baking pan, that is, while it is fresh. But the offerings mingled with oil and the dry ones are eaten by the rest of the priests and their male sons. The baked things given as a portion to the priests, the sons of Aaron, point to the word of God, which is the living spiritual bread that the priest feeds to his children by his teachings to them, and this word is characterized by five attributes that the ways of offering show:

7.4.1.en: 1- Baked in the oven, that is, the fiery word of God issued by the power of the fiery Holy Spirit.

7.4.2.en: 2- Dressed in the frying pan, that is, presented with deep and moving thought.

7.4.3.en: 3- Dressed on a baking pan, that is, a word that reveals the mind of God to man and reveals the mind of man before God.

7.4.4.en: 4- Mingled with oil, that is, accompanied by the power of the Holy Spirit as in the grain offering.

7.4.5.en: 5- Dry, as in the offering that accompanies the sin offering, because sin dries up a person's spiritual life.

7.4.6.en: Thus the priest receives, as Christ receives, the sweet fruits of his children as he receives the dryness of their bitter life, to lead them in every case on the road of salvation.

7.4.7.en: Take care to teach your children the way of God and to care for each one individually, supporting him in his weaknesses and developing his gifts, so that you bind him to the love of Christ and he remains steadfast in the Church.

7.5.s.en: (2) The law of the peace offering

7.5.0.en: The peace offering is of three kinds:

7.5.2.en: 2- The peace offering for a vow (v. 16).

7.5.3.en: 3- The peace offering for a freewill offering (vv. 16-18). And offered with the peace offering:

7.5.4.en: A - An unleavened grain offering, which includes:

7.5.7.en: 3- Fine flour mingled with oil and fried, that is, well mixed, and made into cakes.

7.5.8.en: Of these three kinds some is taken and offered on the altar, because all are unleavened and so signify the pure life free of the evil that leaven signifies.

7.5.9.en: B- Leavened bread is offered with the peace offering to be eaten with this sacrifice, and none of it is offered on the altar, as God stipulated in (ch. 2:11), and this leavened bread also signifies Christ, who bore our sins and then passed through sufferings and death, that is, the fire.

7.5.10.en: These three kinds, that is, the sacrifice and the unleavened and the leavened, are offered as thanksgiving to God for His love and His gifts.

7.6.0.en: Heave offering unto the Lord: lifted up before God and given to the priest.

7.6.1.en: The priest takes for himself one of each kind of food offered with the peace offering, and burns the fat of the sacrifice on the altar and sprinkles its blood around it. The priest's taking of the offerings means, for the one who offers the sacrifice, that he has given God something of his offering, and then the one who offers it eats the rest.

7.7.0.en: The day of his offering: the day of offering the sacrifice with the baked things.

7.7.1.en: The one who offers the sacrifice eats the rest of the flesh on the same day of its offering when it is offered for thanksgiving, that is, none is left until the next day. The first reason is care that the flesh not spoil, and the second is that what is left over is for the poor, because what remains overnight will be burned. This signifies spiritually the necessity of not postponing the immediate enjoyment of the Lord and thanking Him for His gifts, and likewise the necessity of not leaving anything of the Body and Blood of the Lord in the Liturgy until the next day.

7.8.0.en: Voluntary offering: voluntary and not obligatory, that is, a sacrifice offered out of love for God, and it is other than the vow, which is connected with a particular request. If the animal offered as a voluntary offering is lost, it is not replaced, whereas in the case of a vow replacement with one like it is required.

7.8.1.en: The peace offering may be offered either as a vow to God or as an offering of love to Him. In this case it is permitted to eat of it on the first day and the second day of its offering.

7.9.0.en: What remains of the flesh of the voluntary offering or the vow on the third day is burned with fire, so that it may not be exposed to spoiling, and on the other hand so that it may be an encouragement to the one who offers the sacrifice to let the poor share in eating of his sacrifice. It is permitted to eat this sacrifice in the tents of its owners.

7.10.0.en: It shall be an abomination: the sacrifice offered becomes unclean on the third day.

7.10.1.en: The soul .. shall bear his iniquity: the one who offered it sinned and needs to offer a sacrifice so that God may forgive him. The one who breaks God's law and eats on the third day of the peace offering, the following happens to him: 1 - His sacrifice is not accepted.

7.10.2.en: 2- The flesh left until the third day becomes unclean and makes unclean the one who eats it.

7.10.3.en: 3- The one who eats of this flesh and becomes unclean sins and needs to offer a sacrifice so that God may forgive him.

7.11.0.en: Here it stresses two conditions for dealing with the peace offering, which are:

7.11.1.en: 1- The necessity of burning the flesh of the peace offering if it touches anything unclean, and no one eats of it.

7.11.2.en: 2- The one who eats of the peace offering must be clean, that is, with no uncleanness in him such as an issue of blood from him (ch. 15:19).

7.12.0.en: If a person, man or woman, is so bold, while having an uncleanness, whether an issue in a man or an issue of blood in a woman (ch. 15), and eats of the peace offering in violation of God's law, he is cut off from the congregation of the children of Israel and loses his membership and his belonging to the people of God, because he made light of God's law and did not feel his uncleanness and cleanse himself from it. This signifies persisting in sin and then coming forward to partake of the Holy Mysteries, and whoever does this needs severe repentance.

7.13.0.en: If the person is not unclean in his body as in (v. 20), but he made light of it and touched an unclean person or an unclean beast, such as the carcass of a beast or any unclean animal as the Law prescribes (ch. 11:13), then for his making light he is separated and cut off from the people of God.

7.13.1.en: And the touching of uncleanness signifies mixing with the wicked or listening to the teachings of those who have left the Church.

7.14.0.en: God forbids His people to eat the fat of the animals offered as sacrifices, because the fat is set apart for God, so it is not right to trespass upon God's rights, and this signifies the offering of the tithes and the firstfruits to God and not falling short in them.

7.14.1.en: And they may eat the fat of other clean animals of which they do not offer to God, such as gazelles. Likewise the fat mixed with the flesh of the animal of which sacrifices are offered to God.

7.15.0.en: Dead animals and beasts of prey are not offered as sacrifices and are not eaten, but their fat may be used in any works that a person needs, such as lighting.

7.16.0.en: If a person is so bold as to eat of the fat of the sacrifice offered to God and trespasses upon His rights, he is cut off from the people of God, because he defies Him and breaks His law, and the elders of the Jews used to rule that he be whipped 39 stripes if he ate unwittingly, but if he ate deliberately he is cut off as the Law prescribes.

7.17.0.en: He also warns against eating blood as explained before (ch. 3:17), and the one who eats of it is cut off from the people.

7.18.0.en: Wave: he moves it to the east and the west and the north and the south.

7.18.1.en: The one who offers the sacrifice carries on his hands the breast and the right shoulder while sitting before the priest, then he stands before the priest, and the priest places his hands under the hands of the one who offers the sacrifice to lift them with him and move them in the four directions, east and west and north and south, before God.

7.18.2.en: The lifting up of the breast and the right shoulder, that is, offering them to God, and the priest assists him in that, while the waving of them, that is, moving them toward the four directions, is a declaration that God is present everywhere and is the Controller of all, so he offers this sacrifice to Him.

7.19.0.en: After the priest burns the fat of the sacrifice to the Lord on the altar, he takes the breast, and it becomes the portion of all the priests who are in the house of the Lord.

7.20.0.en: The right shoulder: the right front leg.

7.20.1.en: The right shoulder is given to the priest who offers the sacrifice, for it is a heave offering to God who dwells in the heavens, and the priest takes it, so the one who offers it feels that God has accepted a peace offering.

7.21.0.en: This is God's ordinance throughout the generations, that the breast of the sacrifice and the right shoulder be given to the priests to eat, so that the one who offered the sacrifice feels that God has accepted his sacrifice. On the other hand, God provides food for His priests who are consecrated to His service, and there is a relationship of love between the priests and the people.

7.22.0.en: This is also what happens on the day of the anointing of the priest, that is, his being set apart and established as a priest, so the shoulder of the heave offering is given to him and the breast to the priests, as we mentioned in (vv. 30-34), and this is his portion of the peace offering throughout the generations.

7.23.s.en: (3) Summary of chapters six and seven

7.23.0.en: The sacrifice of consecration: the sacrifice offered at the ordination of the priests, by which they fill their hands before God so that they do not stand before the Lord empty, as mentioned in (ch. 6:19-23).

7.23.1.en: God concludes His words about the laws of offering the sacrifices mentioned in the first seven chapters of this book, declaring that this is what God commanded Moses on Mount Sinai when He gave him the laws of the sacrifices.

7.23.2.en: Take care in giving to God, whether to the priests and servants of the Church or to anyone in need, because you give from what God gave you, and God rejoices in your gifts and blesses your life, and you grow in feelings of love and compassion for others.

7.23.29.en: The ritual of the consecration of the priests (1) The consecration of the priests (vv. 1-13:) 1 And the LORD spake unto Moses, saying, 2 Take Aaron and his sons with him, and the garments, and the anointing oil, and a bullock for the sin offering, and two rams, and a basket of unleavened bread; 3 And gather thou all the congregation together unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation. 4 And Moses did as the LORD commanded him; and the assembly was gathered together unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation. 5 And Moses said unto the congregation, This is the thing which the LORD commanded to be done. 6 And Moses brought Aaron and his sons, and washed them with water. 7 And he put upon him the coat, and girded him with the girdle, and clothed him with the robe, and put the ephod upon him, and he girded him with the curious girdle of the ephod, and bound it unto him therewith. 8 And he put the breastplate upon him: also he put in the breastplate the Urim and the Thummim. 9 And he put the mitre upon his head; also upon the mitre, even upon his forefront, did he put the golden plate, the holy crown; as the LORD commanded Moses. 10 And Moses took the anointing oil, and anointed the tabernacle and all that was therein, and sanctified them. 11 And he sprinkled thereof upon the altar seven times, and anointed the altar and all his vessels, both the laver and his foot, to sanctify them. 12 And he poured of the anointing oil upon Aaron's head, and anointed him, to sanctify him. 13 And Moses brought Aaron's sons, and clothed them with coats, and girded them with girdles, and put bonnets upon them; as the LORD commanded Moses.
